cards.front: What is a contextual keyword in Java?
cards.back: A word that acts as a keyword only where the grammar expects it — otherwise it is an ordinary identifier
cards.extra: JLS 3.9 lists 17 contextual keywords (var, yield, record, sealed, permits, module, open, requires, with, and others), versus 51 reserved keywords that can never be identifiers. A reserved keyword is rejected everywhere; a contextual one is rejected only in its own construct.
cards.example:
int var = 1;      // identifier here
var n = 1;          // keyword in a local declaration
class var { }     // error: restricted type name

cards.front: Why is var a reserved type name instead of a reserved keyword?
cards.back: So older code that used var as a variable, method or package name still compiles
cards.extra: JEP 286 chose this deliberately for source compatibility: making var a full keyword would break existing identifiers. The cost is that var cannot name a class or interface — JLS 3.8 excludes permits, record, sealed, var and yield from TypeIdentifier, hence class var {} fails with "'var' not allowed here".
cards.example:
int var = 10;             // old code still compiles
void f(String var) { }      // parameter name: fine
class var { }          // error: 'var' not allowed here

cards.front: Why does an unqualified yield(); fail even when the class declares void yield()?
cards.back: yield is barred as an UnqualifiedMethodIdentifier — qualify it with a receiver or type name
cards.extra: JLS 3.8 forbids yield as an unqualified method identifier so it cannot collide with the switch-expression yield statement. javac: invalid use of a restricted identifier 'yield' (to invoke a method called yield, qualify the yield with a receiver or type name). Declaring the method is fine; calling this.yield() is fine.
cards.example:
void yield() { }
void m() {
    yield();       // error: invalid use of a restricted identifier
    this.yield();  // ok
}

cards.back: Yes — the first var is the keyword, the second is an ordinary identifier
cards.extra: Same spelling, two roles decided by position: a local variable declaration may start with the reserved type name var, and the declarator's name is an Identifier. The result is a String variable named var. Legal but unreadable; the field and parameter spellings are just as legal.
cards.example:
void test() {
    var var = "x";   // compiles, var holds "x"
}
